newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Russian Orthodox fight over Hebron monastery.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian Orthodox fight over Hebron monastery.

text.p: The Cold War isn't over for two opposing branches of Russia's Orthodox Church, who bitterly call each other "reds" and "whites".
While stones and bullets fly in battles between Jews and Arabs in the West bank city of Hebron, the reds and whites are fighting to control the Moslem city's only church.

Their bitter feud dates back to the Russian revolution and dictator Josef Stalin's religious purges that left more than 100,000 dead. The whites, whose leaders went into exile, accuse the reds of collaborating with the communist regime.
The reds counter they had to compromise in order to survive and accuse the whites of abandoning Russia for America.

"It (the Hebron church) is ours. It was made for the Russian people," said Father Mark of the Russian Orthodox Mission of Moscow whose red church had little standing outside the Soviet Union during the Cold War.
The reds expelled the whites by force last Saturday from the Russian Orthodox Monastery of Abraham's Oak in Hebron, helped by a squad of Palestinian police.
Father Mark, who declined to give his last name, says that's just the beginning.
"They are not a church and they represent nobody here," he said, referring to the New York-based whites.
Two elderly nuns were hurt so badly in the fray they had to be taken to hospital.
Sister Juliana Hazbun, 63, stayed in hospital for three days after hitting her head on the stairs during the tumult.
"I have this terrible headache still," she said, adding that the monastery had always belonged to the white Russian Orthodox Church, not the red.
"Their way of behaving is not the way priests behave," said Sister Marina Tchertkoff.
"I was raised to come inside the church with prayers not guns."
HOW THE FIGHT STARTED
The fight over Abraham's Oak began a month ago when Palestinian President Yasser Arafat invited the Russian Orthodox Patriarch to Hebron to visit the church.
The patriarch is a member of the red church, and the monastery's four white monks refused to let him in, according to the monastery's Moslem guard.
"We didn't want to receive them because we don't recognise their church. We didn't know why they came," Tchertkoff said.
Her church sent in five nuns to support the monks.
Meanwhile, the reds complained to the Palestinian police who tried to persuade the whites to share the monastery.
"They said, 'Why don't you live with the reds together,'" Hazbun said. "My first sentence was, 'I will live with the devil before I will live with the reds.'"
Police gave her two options: Live together or get out. Red church leaders said they had obtained an eviction order but Hazbun said she never saw one.
"I fell on the floor and said I won't leave," she said.
"They dragged me like a bag of potatoes. It was shameful. My dress went up. I was very shy that men were looking at my seat. It was so humiliating, I thought I would die," she said.
Women police officers threw her out the door, where she hit her head on the steps, she said. Outside, she found two of the four monks handcuffed and beaten.
Israeli officials say the Palestinians may have intervened to ingratiate themselves with the Russian government.
The reds control most church property in Israel, but the whites own churches in the West Bank, dating back to when Jordan recognised them as rightful heirs to the Russian Orthodox Church.
When Israel captured the area in the 1967 Middle East war, it left the property untouched. But Palestinians, who took over in January, want to give it back.
"Arafat wanted to give the church, the monastery, all this property to the red church," said David Bar-Illan, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"He is trying to curry favor with the red church, which is part of the Russian regime, while the white church is part of a church formed abroad," he said.
Palestinian officials denied the allegations.
"The Israeli government is making its allegations to drive a wedge among Palestinians," Ahmed Abdel Rahman, secretary general of Palestinian Authority, told Reuters.
Now, three monks and five nuns from the Moscow-based red branch of the Russian Orthodox Church run the monastery. The white branch wants it back.
CHURCHES SPLIT AFTER COMMUNIST REVOLUTION
The white and red branches of the Russian Orthodox Church split early this century after Russia's 1917 Bolshevik Revolution.
Many of the whites went into exile after Stalin sent 100,000 bishops, priests and faithful to their deaths in Siberian labour camps in 1946.
But the reds survived the atheist regime by compromising with the communist authorities.
The whites say they'll never forgive them for it.
"They don't recognise the people who were killed by the communists as martyrs. Their church was restored by Stalin," Tchertkoff said.
"Since that time...they didn't recognise that their church is built on something false," she said.
But the reds say the whites aren't even a church.
"This church, the Russian Orthodox Church Abroad, they are recognised by no one. They represent no one anywhere," said Father Mark.
His red church has experienced a revival in Russia since the fall of communism and wants to reclaim other property abroad lost during the communist years.

"From our point of view, they are not the owners of the churches and monasteries in the Mount of Olives and Jericho and Gethsemane and another church, St. Alexandranevsky, in the Old City of Jerusalem," Father Mark said.
"We don't recognise anybody else as the owner, and we want to get it back."
